content: The document titled Preventing Surgical Site Infections: Implementation Approaches for Evidence-Based Recommendations was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2018. Professional editing assistance was provided by Rosemary Sudan. The document highlights the global burden of surgical site infections (SSIs), particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where up to one-third of surgical patients may be affected. In African countries, SSIs are a common complication, with up to 20% of women undergoing cesarean sections developing postoperative wound infections. In higher-income settings, SSIs are the second most frequent healthcare-associated infection (HAI) in Europe and the United States, contributing to significant morbidity, prolonged hospital stays, and increased healthcare costs. Preventing SSIs is complex due to multiple risk factors throughout the surgical patient journey, including post-discharge. However, up to half of SSIs can be prevented through the implementation of evidence-based clinical practice guidelines using a multimodal improvement strategy. Despite this, no healthcare facility or country is free from avoidable infections, and many lack the necessary infrastructure or established infection prevention and control (IPC) programs. The WHO guidelines on core components of IPC programs include SSI prevention as a critical element for improving patient outcomes. These guidelines are designed to be globally applicable and adaptable to local contexts, considering scientific evidence, cost implications, and patient preferences. The document also references updated evidence-based recommendations from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued in 2017. The document aims to provide practical examples and tested approaches for successful SSI prevention implementation at the facility level. It emphasizes the importance of a multimodal strategy, which requires understanding the local context and addressing barriers to implementation. The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist is presented as a global example of improving surgical safety, including SSI prevention, through effective implementation and dissemination. The target audience includes professionals involved in surgical care and IPC, such as surgeons, surgical nurses, patient safety teams, and quality improvement teams. The document outlines key barriers, challenges, and success stories, offering insights and checklists to guide SSI prevention strategies. It aims to stimulate targeted improvement steps regardless of the healthcare facility's level of progress, ultimately contributing to safer surgical care worldwide.
